name: Follicle-stimulating hormone
rangeNote: No population range is built in: normal values depend on sex, age, the phase of the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause, and on the assay and its calibration. FSH varies from cycle to cycle during the menopausal transition, so a single value is hard to interpret. Use your lab's printed range and, for women, the cycle day.
summary: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is released by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. In women it helps eggs mature in the ovaries; in men it supports sperm production in the testes.

high.meaning: A higher FSH usually means the pituitary is pushing harder because the ovaries or testes are not responding well. It rises as the menopausal transition proceeds and stays high after menopause. Read together with LH (luteinising hormone) and estradiol or testosterone. Discuss unexpected results with your doctor.
commonCauses: Damage to the testes from injury, infection, chemotherapy or radiation, or conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome
Clomiphene or similar medicines, which raise FSH

low.meaning: A low FSH can mean reduced signalling from the pituitary or hypothalamus, or that the body's own signal is switched off by hormones from outside. Discuss unexpected results with your doctor.
commonCauses: Testosterone treatment, anabolic steroids or SARMs (selective androgen receptor modulators), which suppress FSH and sperm production
Hormonal contraceptives, estrogen treatment and GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analogues
Low energy availability from very low food intake or very heavy training
Pituitary or hypothalamus conditions, high prolactin
Polycystic ovary syndrome, where FSH is often in the normal to low-normal range
